c.tagline: Colonial forts, cobblestone lanes, and Caribbean rhythm on a walled Atlantic bay.

taxi.fareNote: Official white 'Taxi Turístico' cabs are metered, but posted flat tourist-zone rates from the airport and cruise port to Old San Juan, Condado, and Isla Verde are standard. Uber is available and often cheaper than a taxi.

emergency.note: 911 is the island-wide emergency line covering police, fire, and medical.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Santurce: La Placita de Santurce, San Juan

avoid.reason: Old San Juan/Condado safe; caution near public housing (caseríos) and La Perla after dark; petty theft

hood_desc: The 500-year-old walled colonial core on a headland, packed with pastel Spanish townhouses, cobbled blue-stone streets, and the massive El Morro and San Cristóbal forts; the most atmospheric and walkable base for first-timers.
An upscale beachfront strip of high-rise hotels, designer shops, casinos, and oceanfront restaurants along Ashford Avenue; suits travelers wanting sand, nightlife, and dining steps from their room.
A gritty-turned-arty district of street murals, galleries, and the La Placita market square that becomes the city's best bar and club scene after dark; draws a younger, creative crowd.
A resort-lined beach zone right by the airport, with wide golden sands, casinos, and big-name hotels; convenient and relaxed, good for beach-focused stays and quick arrivals.
A quieter, leafy residential neighborhood of restored mansions, boutique hotels, and the convention district just south of Condado; calmer and more local in feel.

water.note: Tap water meets US standards and is safe to drink in San Juan.

transit.pay: The Tren Urbano and AMA buses share a contactless fare card sold at Tren Urbano stations; a single ride runs about $0.75-$1.50. The Old San Juan trolley is free, and the AcuaExpreso ferry to Cataño costs about $0.50, paid in cash or card.
transit.hours: Tren Urbano runs roughly 5:30 AM to 11:30 PM; AMA buses run daytime hours with limited frequency and little night service, so most visitors rely on Uber or taxis after dark.
transit.note: Public transit is limited and doesn't directly serve the main tourist zones - the single Tren Urbano line skirts the inland suburbs and never reaches Old San Juan, Condado, or the beaches, so Uber, taxis, and the free Old San Juan trolley are how most visitors actually get around.

food.name: Mofongo
food.desc: Green plantain fried and mashed with garlic, olive oil and chicharron in a wooden pilon, then stuffed with shrimp, conch, roast pork or ropa vieja.

places.name: Deaverdura
places.note: Small daily-changing criollo kitchen; the mofongo with lechon and chimichurri is the order.

places.name: Raices
places.note: Traditional Puerto Rican menu served in pilones and enamel cups; touristy but consistently good.

places.name: Bebo's Cafe
places.note: Neighbourhood diner where locals eat; big stuffed mofongos at reasonable prices.

food.name: Lechon asado
food.desc: Whole pig rubbed with adobo and turned over coals for hours until the skin shatters. Best eaten by the pound with rice and boiled green bananas.

places.name: Ruta del Lechon
places.note: The Pork Highway an hour south of San Juan; open-air lechoneras, live music, weekend crowds.

places.name: El Cuerito de la 15
places.note: City lechonera known for well-seasoned roast pork and crisp skin at fair prices.

places.name: Casita Miramar
places.note: Modern cocina criolla in an old house; roast pork and daily specials, no reservations.

food.name: Alcapurrias
food.desc: Fritters of grated green banana and yautia wrapped around seasoned ground beef or crab, fried to order. The classic Pinones beach snack.

places.name: Kiosko El Boricua
places.note: Widely rated the best alcapurrias in Pinones, crisp outside and fried the moment you order.

places.name: Pinones kiosks
places.note: Dozens of seaside chinchorros minutes from San Juan; a full afternoon costs very little.

places.name: El Cuerito de la 15
places.note: In-city alternative for alcapurrias, pastelillos and bacalaitos without the drive.

food.name: Bacalaitos
food.desc: Saltcod fritters flattened into crisp, lacy discs the size of a plate. Afro-Puerto Rican street food eaten hot from the fryer with beer.

places.name: Pinones kiosks
places.note: The heartland of bacalaitos and empanadillas, eaten at plastic tables facing the sea.

places.name: El Cuerito de la 15
places.note: Fritters fried through the day alongside the roast pork; easy stop before La Placita.

places.name: La Placita de Santurce
places.note: Market square with fritter counters by day and a huge street party by night.

food.name: Arroz con gandules and pernil
food.desc: Sofrito-stained rice with pigeon peas beside slow-roasted pork shoulder. The Sunday table and holiday centrepiece of Puerto Rican home cooking.

places.name: Casita Miramar
places.note: Chalkboard menu of grandmother-style criollo dishes; among San Juan's most loved kitchens.

places.name: Deaverdura
places.note: Daily home-cooked plates for a fraction of Old San Juan prices; arrive before the rice runs out.

places.name: Raices
places.note: Full criollo spread including gandules rice, pernil and tostones in one sitting.

food.name: Pina colada
food.desc: Rum, coconut cream and pineapple, invented in San Juan in the 1950s and still argued over. Two bars claim the original recipe.

places.name: Barrachina
places.note: Claims the invention; churned constantly on a chilled machine so it needs no added ice.

places.name: Caribar at Caribe Hilton
places.note: The rival claim, dated 1954; the bar serves four versions tracing the drink's evolution.

places.name: Pinones kiosks
places.note: Beach-shack coladas served in plastic cups for a fraction of the hotel-bar price.

food.name: Puerto Rican rum
food.desc: The island distils most of the rum sold in the United States. Drink it straight, in a coquito at Christmas, or in a well-made old fashioned.

places.name: La Factoria
places.note: Warren of hidden bar rooms behind an unmarked door; internationally ranked cocktail list.

places.name: Casa Bacardi
places.note: Short ferry ride across the bay for distillery tours, tastings and mixology classes.

places.name: La Placita de Santurce
places.note: Local bars around the market plaza pouring rum drinks; liveliest Thursday to Saturday.

landmarks: Castillo San Felipe del Morro
A massive 16th-century Spanish fortress on a rocky promontory, one of the most iconic and photographed sights in the Caribbean.
Castillo San Cristóbal
The largest fortification built by Spain in the Americas, with sweeping ramparts and panoramic views over Old San Juan.
La Fortaleza
The oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas, a UNESCO-listed governor's residence overlooking San Juan Bay.
Calle Fortaleza (Old San Juan streets)
A postcard-perfect cobblestone street draped in colorful umbrellas and pastel colonial facades.
Puerta de San Juan (City Gate)
The last surviving gate of the old city walls, a striking blue-and-white archway leading into the historic quarter.
Catedral de San Juan Bautista
The second-oldest cathedral in the Americas, home to the tomb of explorer Juan Ponce de León.
Paseo de la Princesa
A scenic tree-lined promenade along the old city walls, dotted with fountains, art, and bay views.
La Perla
A vibrant seaside neighborhood tucked beneath the city walls, famous for its colorful houses and as the setting of the "Despacito" video.
Plaza de Armas
The historic main square of Old San Juan, ringed by government buildings and a lively spot for people-watching.
El Capitolio (Capitol of Puerto Rico)
A grand neoclassical marble capitol building topped with a mosaic-tiled dome overlooking the Atlantic.

train.note: Puerto Rico is an island, so there are no international or intercity trains and no rail link to the US mainland. The only passenger railway is the Tren Urbano, a 17 km, 16-station automated metro run by Alternate Concepts for the Puerto Rico Department of Transportation and Public Works, linking Bayamón and Guaynabo with Santurce-side San Juan at Sagrado Corazón. It does not reach Old San Juan, the cruise piers or Luis Muñoz Marín airport, so you will need a connecting AMA bus, the T5 shuttle or a taxi. Fares are low and paid with a contactless card at the gates.

bus.note: There are no international buses to or from Puerto Rico. Within San Juan, AMA operates the city bus network and the Metro Urbano bus rapid transit corridor to Bayamón, with the T5 route linking Old San Juan, the cruise piers and the Isla Verde hotel strip. For the rest of the island, carros públicos - shared vans - leave from the Río Piedras terminal beside the Tren Urbano station to Ponce, Fajardo, Mayagüez and smaller towns; they run mostly in the morning, depart when full, take cash and cannot be booked ahead. Coverage is patchy enough that most visitors going beyond the metro area hire a car.

intl.to: Santo Domingo (Dominican Republic) - overnight car and passenger ferry from the San Juan port area
Vieques & Culebra (Puerto Rico) - sails from the Ceiba terminal, about an hour east of San Juan
Cataño (Puerto Rico) - Acuaexpreso commuter ferry from Pier 2, Old San Juan

ferry.note: Ferries del Caribe runs an overnight car-and-passenger ferry between San Juan and Santo Domingo several times a week, taking around 12 hours with cabins available; it is a full international crossing, so you need a passport and must clear immigration at both ends, and vehicles must be booked well in advance. The Vieques and Culebra ferries no longer leave from Fajardo town but from the purpose-built terminal at Ceiba, roughly an hour's drive east of San Juan, and seats should be reserved online because residents get priority. The short Acuaexpreso hop from Pier 2 in Old San Juan across the bay to Cataño takes under 10 minutes and is the usual way to reach the Bacardí distillery. There is no ferry link to the US mainland or to the US Virgin Islands from San Juan itself.

half.name: El Yunque National Forest
half.blurb: The only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest system, with waterfalls, trails, and lookout towers, an hour east of the city.

half.name: Bacardí Distillery (Casa Bacardí)
half.blurb: The world's largest premium rum distillery, across the bay in Cataño and reachable by the AcuaExpreso ferry, with tastings and tours.

half.name: Piñones
half.blurb: A beachside stretch of Afro-Puerto Rican food kiosks and mangrove bike trails just east of Isla Verde.

full.name: Fajardo & Bioluminescent Bay
full.blurb: East-coast marina town and gateway to Laguna Grande's glowing bioluminescent waters and boat trips to nearby cays.

full.name: Ponce
full.blurb: The elegant 'Pearl of the South,' with neoclassical plazas, the striped Parque de Bombas firehouse, and a fine-art museum.

full.name: Camuy River Cave Park & Arecibo
full.blurb: A vast limestone cave system on the northwest karst, near the site of the giant former Arecibo radio telescope.
